label: Jude 1:1–2
text:
"Servant" (doulos) opens the letter with bondslave, not blood relation — Jude identifies himself as "brother of James" rather than brother of the Lord, a striking, deliberate humility given his actual family connection.

"Sanctified" and "preserved" are both perfect passive participles, hēgiasmenois and tetērēmenois — a setting-apart and a keeping both already accomplished and, in the present, still standing in full force.

"Preserved" repeats tēreō, a root this short letter will return to again and again — applied here, at the opening, to believers being kept safe, and later, ominously, to fallen angels kept instead for judgment.

"Multiplied" is the same optative wish-form, plēthyntheiē, opening both of Peter's letters — a shared epistolary convention among these closely related early Christian writings.
translation: Jude, a slave of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, to those who have been called, who have been loved in God the Father, and have been kept for Jesus Christ: may mercy and peace and love be multiplied to you.

label: Jude 1:3–4
text:
"Gave all diligence" (spoudēn poioumenos) describes an eager haste to write about shared salvation, a plan Jude abandons mid-thought for a more urgent one — the letter he intended and the letter he actually sends are not the same, by his own admission.

"Earnestly contend" is epagōnizesthai, a rare, intensive compound built on agōn, "a contest, a struggle" — the direct root of the English "agony" — casting the defense of the faith as a strenuous, exhausting athletic or gladiatorial fight, not a calm intellectual defense.

"Once delivered" translates hapax paradotheisē — hapax means "once, and for all time," marking the apostolic deposit of faith as complete and closed, not an evolving body of teaching still open to revision.

"Crept in unawares" is pareisedysan, a rare compound literally meaning "to slip in stealthily alongside" — the vocabulary of infiltration, matching almost exactly the language 2 Peter uses of the same danger.

"Before of old ordained" is progegrammenoi, perfect passive, "written about beforehand" — these men's coming judgment is treated as something already recorded in advance, not a surprise improvised after the fact.
translation: Beloved, making all haste to write to you concerning our common salvation, I found it necessary to write to you, urging you to be contending earnestly for the faith once for all delivered to the saints. Because certain men have slipped in stealthily, those long ago written up beforehand for this judgment, ungodly ones, turning the grace of our God into licentiousness, and denying our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.

label: Jude 1:5–7
text:
Three examples run in a row — Israel destroyed in unbelief despite being delivered, angels who abandoned their proper place, Sodom and Gomorrah — closely paralleling the same triad in 2 Peter 2, likely drawing on shared early Christian teaching material.

"Kept not" (mē tērēsantas) plays directly against "he hath reserved" (tetērēken) two clauses later — the identical tēreō root used both of what the angels failed to keep, their own proper domain, and of the chains in which God now keeps them instead.

"First estate" is archēn, "beginning, original rank" — their own proper sphere of authority, abandoned for "another habitation" not their own.

"Strange flesh" (sarkos heteras) likely names the attempted assault in Genesis 19, sexual pursuit outside the boundaries fixed at creation, echoing the same disordered crossing of natural boundaries already described of the angels one verse earlier.

"Set forth for an example" is deigma prokeintai, "lie publicly on display" — the ruined cities themselves are pictured as a permanent exhibit, still standing as visible evidence long after the event.
translation: But I want to remind you, though you know all things once for all, that the Lord, having saved a people out of the land of Egypt, the second time destroyed those not believing; and angels who did not keep their own domain, but abandoned their own dwelling place, he has kept in eternal chains under gloom for the judgment of the great day; as Sodom and Gomorrah, and the cities around them, in the same manner as these, having given themselves over to fornication and having gone after strange flesh, are set forth as an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire.

label: Jude 1:8–10
text:
"Filthy dreamers" translates enypniazomenoi, present participle, "dreaming" — these men are pictured as living inside a self-generated fantasy, detached from the real world, possibly also claiming false visionary experiences to authorize their teaching.

"Despise dominion" uses athetousin, "to set aside, nullify" — the same legal verb used elsewhere for annulling a covenant or contract, here applied to a wholesale rejection of legitimate authority.

The dispute between Michael and the devil "about the body of Moses" is drawn from a Jewish tradition outside the Old Testament canon, likely the lost Testament of Moses — Jude cites it as familiar background his readers would already recognize, not as a claim that it belongs to Scripture itself.

"Durst not" is ouk etolmēsen, "did not dare" — even the greatest of angels, disputing with Satan himself over the highest of stakes, refrains from the very "railing accusation" these false teachers indulge in freely against beings far above them.

"Corrupt themselves" is phtheirontai, present passive — a continuous, ongoing self-destruction, the identical phthora root that runs through 2 Peter's vocabulary for decay.
translation: Yet in the same manner also these, dreaming, are defiling the flesh, and are setting aside lordship, and are blaspheming glorious ones. But Michael the archangel, when disputing with the devil, arguing about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring against him a judgment of blasphemy, but said, The Lord rebuke you. But these blaspheme whatever things they do not know, and whatever things they understand by instinct, as the irrational animals, in these things they are being corrupted.

label: Jude 1:11–13
text:
Three Old Testament figures stack up as a rhetorical drumbeat — Cain, whose false worship led to murder; Balaam, the prophet for hire; Korah, whose rebellion against God's appointed order swallowed him alive — each name doing the work of an entire argument in a single word.

"Spots" most likely mistranslates spilades, a rare word for hidden reefs, a maritime hazard lurking just under the surface — a different, similarly spelled word from the "spots" (spiloi) used of blemishes in 2 Peter, and one that fits far better with the storm-driven clouds and shipwreck imagery surrounding it.

"Feeding themselves" is heautous poimainontes, literally "shepherding themselves" — the shepherd-verb turned inside out: men who exist to feed the flock instead feed only themselves at the flock's own shared meals.

"Twice dead, plucked up by the roots" (ekrizōthenta) pictures a tree not merely barren but uprooted entirely — dead in its origin and now removed past any possibility of ever growing again.

"Wandering stars" is asteres planētai, the direct root of the English "planet" — lights that have left their fixed, appointed course, kept, like the angels of verse 6, for a darkness that never lifts.
translation: Woe to them, because they went the way of Cain, and gave themselves over to the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the rebellion of Korah. These are hidden reefs in your love feasts, feasting together with you without fear, shepherding themselves; clouds without water, carried along by winds; autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shameful deeds; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever.

label: Jude 1:14–16
text:
Jude quotes 1 Enoch directly, a Jewish work outside the Old Testament canon — his use of it as accurate prophecy has been much discussed, but the citation functions here as an appeal to already-familiar material, not a claim about that book's own inspired status.

"Ungodly" and its cognates repeat four times within a single verse in the Greek — a hammering, deliberate repetition driving the word itself into the reader's ear.

"Convince" is elenxai, courtroom vocabulary for convicting or exposing — the coming judgment is framed as a formal legal reckoning, not a vague reckoning of scores.

"Murmurers, complainers" translates gongystai and mempsimoiroi — gongystai is onomatopoeic, mimicking the very sound of low, continuous grumbling, while mempsimoiroi, "blaming one's lot," names a person chronically dissatisfied with the very portion assigned to him.

"Having men's persons in admiration because of advantage" describes calculated flattery — admiring faces specifically, and only, for what can be gotten from them.
translation: And Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied concerning these, saying, Behold, the Lord came with his holy myriads, to execute judgment against all, and to convict all the ungodly concerning all their works of ungodliness which they did in an ungodly way, and concerning all the harsh things which ungodly sinners spoke against him. These are grumblers, finding fault with their lot, going according to their own lusts, and their mouth speaks bombastic things, admiring faces for the sake of advantage.

label: Jude 1:17–19
text:
"Mockers" is empaiktai, the identical rare word 2 Peter uses of the scoffers who will come "in the last days" — the same warning, in the same vocabulary, given independently by two separate apostolic witnesses.

"Separate themselves" translates a rare compound, apodiorizontes, "to mark off boundary lines for oneself" — describing men who set themselves apart as a distinct, superior clique rather than genuinely dividing the sound from the unsound.

"Sensual" is psychikoi, "soulish" — operating on the merely natural, unregenerate level, the identical term Paul applies to the man who cannot receive the things of the Spirit.

"Having not the Spirit" states, without qualification, the plainest possible test: whatever spiritual claims such men make for themselves, the Spirit's actual presence is flatly denied them.
translation: But you, beloved, remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, that they told you, In the last time there will be mockers, going according to their own ungodly lusts. These are the ones marking off divisions, soulish, not having the Spirit.

label: Jude 1:20–23
text:
"Building up" is epoikodomountes, present participle — a continuous, ongoing construction upon a foundation, "your most holy faith," already laid and not itself in need of rebuilding.

"Keep" is tērēsate, aorist imperative — the same tēreō root that has run through the whole letter, now turned from a description of what God does for believers into a direct command for what believers must do themselves.

"Making a difference" most naturally describes the wavering, doubting people themselves who need compassion, rather than a call to discernment on the rescuer's part — mercy shown precisely to those still caught between belief and doubt.

"Pulling...out of the fire" is harpazontes, "snatching, seizing forcibly" — urgent, decisive rescue, not a gentle invitation extended at leisure.

"Garment spotted by the flesh" pictures even the clothing that has merely touched corruption as something to regard with fear — rescue is urged alongside real caution against contamination, not naive fearlessness.
translation: But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. And have mercy on some, those who are doubting; but others save, snatching them out of the fire; and on others have mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.

label: Jude 1:24–25
text:
"Keep...from falling" translates phylaxai aptaistous — phylassō, a close synonym of tēreō, "to guard," paired with aptaistous, "without stumbling" — a striking closing assurance, given every fall and stumble catalogued throughout the letter's false teachers.

"Present" is stēsai, "to set standing, to establish" — believers are pictured not merely surviving to the end but positioned, upright, in a stable, secure stance.

"Faultless" is amōmous, sacrificial vocabulary for an offering without blemish, the same standard applied elsewhere to Christ himself, now applied to those he presents.

"With exceeding joy" is en agalliasei, the same intensive, exultant joy-word Peter uses of believers rejoicing even now — carried here into the very moment of final presentation before God's glory.
translation: Now to him who is able to guard you without stumbling, and to set you standing, unblemished, in the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, before all time, and now, and unto all the ages. Amen.
